entry.title: How to Scan Custom ABAP for Security Issues in Eclipse (Step-by-Step)
entry.content:
Disclosure: I work on this tool at RedRays. This post is a straightforward setup guide, not a product pitch.

This post walks through connecting Eclipse to a static analysis backend that scans custom ABAP for common security issues (SQL injection, missing authorization checks, hard-coded credentials, weak crypto, and similar) and returns findings directly in the IDE.

Prerequisites

- Eclipse 2024-09 or newer
- SAP ABAP Development Tools (ADT) installed
- Java 17
- Network access to the backend you plan to scan against (in this walkthrough, a demo instance)

Step 1: Get an API key

The plugin needs an API key to authenticate against a scan backend. For testing, there's a self-service demo instance:

1. Open get.abap-security.com.
2. Enter a name and email address.
3. Click Create my Eclipse API key.
4. Copy the key immediately - it is displayed once.

 

Notes on the demo instance:
- Limited to one key per IP address per time window.
- It is a shared instance - do not submit confidential or production code to it. For real use, point the plugin at your own tenant or an on-premise instance instead (see "Beyond the demo" below).

Step 2: Install the plugin

In Eclipse:

1. Help → Install New Software…
2. Click Add… and enter the update site: plugin.abap-security.com
3. Select RedRays ABAP Scanner from the list.
4. Finish the wizard and restart Eclipse when prompted.

Step 3: Configure the connection

1. Window → Preferences → RedRays Scanner
2. Set Working mode to RedRays.
3. Set RedRays URL to https://demo.abap-security.com:8443/ (or your own instance's URL).
4. Paste the API key from Step 1 into RedRays API key.
5. Click Test connection and confirm it succeeds before continuing.

 

Step 4: Run a scan

1. Right-click any ABAP object in the Project Explorer.
2. Select Scan with RedRays.
3. Choose the Quick scan profile for a first run.
4. Findings appear in a dedicated Eclipse view as the scan completes.

Reading the results

- Findings are grouped by severity: Critical, High, Medium, Low.
- Double-clicking a finding opens the source at the exact line.
- Each finding includes a CVSS score and an automated exploitability check, intended to reduce false positives that would otherwise need manual triage.

Categories currently covered include: SQL/ADBC injection, OS command execution, dynamic WHERE/ORDER BY clauses, path traversal on OPEN DATASET, RFC trust issues, missing AUTHORITY-CHECK, hard-coded credentials, and weak cryptographic algorithms (MD5/SHA-1), among others.

Beyond the demo

The same plugin can point at a privately provisioned tenant or an on-premise instance instead of the shared demo, with isolated access per subaccount and no source retention (code is scanned in memory and discarded; only findings are stored). There is also a REST API for scanning from CI/CD, including an endpoint that returns an allow/block decision for a transport based on a severity threshold - useful as a pre-import gate.

Resources

- Plugin overview: redrays.io/abap-scanner-eclipse-plugin
- Demo / API key: get.abap-security.com

entry.title: Support Accreditation Unit 2 Lesson: Resolving Issues with Troubleshooting and Diagnostic Tools
entry.content:
This blog provides concise details on various troubleshooting and diagnostics tools to enable you to solve challenges across your SAP landscape. This is an excerpt from the Support Accreditation learning course Unit 2 Lesson 2. The tools we will deep-dive into are:

  • Support Log Assistant
  • Automated Search for SAP Notes
  • Performance Assistant for SAP Notes and SAP Knowledge Base Articles Search
  • Kernel Snapshot Analyzer
  • SAP BusinessObjects BI Support Tool
  • Flexible Log Reader

Ready to level up your SAP support journey? Get Support Accredited and unlock the full power of self-service tools, expert tips, and multi-channels. Earn an SAP-certified digital badge to showcase your expertise.  Begin your Support Accreditation journey today!

 

Support Log Assistant

Overview

  • The support log assistant tool analyses text files such as logs, traces, and configuration files automatically for known issues and recommendations.
  • On the SAP for Me customer portal, the support log assistant analysis is activated during case creation, when troubleshooting files are attached.
  • It is also freely available as a standalone self-service web application, powered by the SAP Business Technology Platform, scan log/trace files in your web browser.
  • Identifies log issues and provides references to relevant SAP Notes and SAP Knowledge Base Articles.

Benefits

  • 24/7 automated, expert-level log file analysis.
  • Accelerated issue resolution without the need to open a support case.
  • Save time by reducing manual log analysis and solution searches.
  • Generates a PDF report of log analysis findings and recommendations.
  • Easily share results with peers to extend best practices and lessons learned.

Access

When you create a case and attach files to it in the "Attachments" section, support log assistant analysis occurs automatically. You can also access the support log assistant as a standalone tool by either:

  • Choosing the "Services & Support" dashboard in SAP for Me.
  • Using this link to connect directly to the standalone tool.

 

You can then use the support log assistant effectively by following the steps below:

  1. Add log files.

     

  2. To scan files, choose Next.

     

  3. Review raised alerts and suggested solutions.

     

  4. Provide feedback on the efficacy of the analysis.

     

  5. Download the "Analysis Report" and "Archive Session Files" if you want to save or share the analysis results.

     

Relevant Links

  • Support log assistant standalone, self-service tool
  • Support log assistant video demo
  • SAP Knowledge Base Article: 2838708 - Using the support log assistant to automate support-related file analysis
  • SAP Help Portal: Support log assistant Wiki
  • List of File Types that can be Analyzed

 

Automated Search for SAP Notes

Overview

  • The Automated Notes Search Tool (ANST) simplifies the identification of SAP correction notes for functional issues, customer codes, and customizing tables, particularly for standard processes.
  • To access SAP-relevant notes and identify issues related to customer code and customizing tables, users can initiate the process by starting the ANST transaction.
  • Additional resources are available for further understanding, including FAQs, instructional videos, and the SAP Help Portal.
  • Explore the following blogs for more insights: ANST and What is ANST?

Benefits

  • The tool only identifies SAP Notes that are relevant to the specific issue, streamlining the search process.
  • Unlike traditional note searches that require specific search terms, this tool automatically searches for SAP Notes based on the ABAP objects involved in the process, simplifying the search.
  • The tool is designed for ABAP-based systems, whether they run directly in the back-end system or through a front end, such as SAP Fiori or portals.

Access

  • Start an ANST transaction from the back-end and reproduce the issue. You can find more information in SAP Knowledge Base Article 1818192.
  • Before you proceed, make sure that the following notes is implemented in your system:2286869. Probably, the note has been applied by support package but manual steps have to be followed anyway.

 

 

Performance Assistant for SAP Notes and SAP Knowledge Base Articles Search

Overview

  • The Performance Assistant simplifies the search for SAP Notes and SAP Knowledge Base Articles related to ABAP messages. It's based on the relevant message code, including the message class and number.
  • For additional information, you can check the FAQ, watch an informative video, or access in-depth details in the blog.

Benefits

  • Receive real-time updates for documentation.
  • The Performance Assistant instantly identifies new SAP Notes containing the relevant ABAP message code, ensuring you benefit from immediate updates and information.

Access

  • When you encounter an error message, double-click the error message and, to proceed with additional actions, choose the binoculars or search icon.
  • For more detailed guidance on this process, you can find additional information in SAP Knowledge Base Article 2096401.

 

 

Kernel Snapshot Analyzer

Overview

  • Server snapshots can be triggered automatically or manually.
  • The kernel snapshot analyzer runs over 36 analyzers for different scenarios.
  • Read a blog introducing kernel snapshot and kernel snapshot analyzer on SAP Community.
  • SAP Knowledge Base Article 3110588 explains how the kernel snapshot analyzer helps analyze system-wide issues and provides solutions using server snapshots.

Benefits

  • The tool gathers the most important trace files used for troubleshooting.
  • It streamlines the analysis of ABAP system-wide problems, such as system hang-ups, slow performance, resource bottlenecks, and high business load situations.
  • Additionally, it visualizes errors and provides solutions along with configuration recommendations.

Access

  • A Java-based application is available for download from SAP Knowledge Base Article 3110588.
  • SAP Knowledge Base Article 3122914 provides a step-by-step guide to collecting a server snapshot and analyzing it with the kernel snapshot analyzer.

 

 

SAP BusinessObjects BI Support Tool

Overview

  • The SAP BusinessObjects BI support tool is a simple and easy-to-deploy client for the SAP BusinessObjects BI platform.
  • Its landscape analysis report offers a comprehensive view of the configuration and topology of SAP Business Objects Business Intelligence.
  • The tool automatically checks for SAP Best Practices, system configuration, service distribution, and other alerts.
  • It includes a toolbox with various root cause analysis and administrative tools, making it a lightweight supportability solution that simplifies the work of BI administrators.

Benefits

  • It eliminates question ping-pong and speeds up issue resolution.
  • Historical system configuration capture and change analysis are supported.
  • Admins save time with built-in tools, such as security analyser, authentication, and trace wizards.
  • Proactive issue identification is enabled through customizable landscape alerts.
  • Sensitive report data can be secured for enhanced security.

Access

  • The tool is free for all SAP BusinessObjects customers and can be downloaded via the Software Download Center.
  • Additional information and resources can be found on the SAP Help Portal.
  • There is a version 2.1 webinar and demo available for further insights and demonstrations.

 

 

Flexible Log Reader

Overview

  • A versatile log reading application for analyzing text log files, regardless of their source application
  • Designed for SAP BI platform trace logs (GLFs) and other text formats
  • Features powerful search and filtering options
  • Includes configuration files and expert-created plugins that facilitate automatic analysis and tagging for quick access to critical information
  • A versatile log reading application for analyzing text log files, regardless of their source application

Benefits

  • Uses pre-built categories for quick identification of common SAP BusinessObjects BI log messages.
  • Can efficiently read long chains of multiple logs with minimal memory usage.
  • Capable of opening and scanning large logs, often exceeding the available memory on the machine. For example, a 4GB machine can load approximately 18GB of logs.

Access

  • No installation is required. Download and extract the ZIP file.
  • Run the tool by double-clicking 'FlexiLogReader64.exe'.
  • You can download it from Flexible Log Reader on the SAP Help Portal.

 

Relevant Links

  • SAP KBA 1818192: FAQ for Automated Note Search Tool (ANST)
  • SAP KBA 2096401: FAQ for PANKS
  • SAP KBA 3110588: Kernel snapshot analyzer
  • SAP KBA 2138275: How to generate a landscape analysis report
  • SAP KBA 2203047: How to read and analyze log files

 

Thanks to all the experts from Global Customer Support for putting this content together!

entry.title: Building a Production-Ready Custom ATC Check: Enforcing ABAP Unit Coverage
entry.content:
Introduction

Many development teams encourage ABAP Unit adoption, but enforcing minimum test coverage is still a challenge.

During a recent project, I needed a way to prevent the release of new developments that did not meet a minimum coverage threshold.

Since I couldn't find a standard ATC check that fulfilled this requirement, I decided to build a custom ATC validation.

The final solution became a lightweight and configurable quality gate that can be integrated directly into existing SCI and ATC processes.

Inspiration

Before starting the implementation, I analyzed several open-source ATC extensions, especially the SAP Code Pal for ABAP project.

Code Pal is an excellent reference for understanding how custom checks can be integrated into the ATC framework and how configurable validations can be implemented.

However, my goal was not to build a generic quality framework. Instead, I wanted a lightweight solution focused on a single requirement: enforcing a minimum ABAP Unit test coverage threshold.

For this reason, I implemented a simplified check that leverages the standard SCI/ATC framework and ABAP Unit coverage APIs while remaining easy to maintain and extend.

Understanding the Solution

The solution is composed of three main components:

  • A custom ATC category
  • A custom ATC check
  • A configurable SCI/ATC variant

The execution flow is illustrated below:

SCI / ATC
      ↓
Custom Check
      ↓
ABAP Unit Coverage Analysis
      ↓
Threshold Validation
      ↓
ATC Finding

Creating a Custom Check Category

The first step is to create a custom category that will group all checks.

Create a class that inherits from CL_CI_CATEGORY_ROOT.

METHOD constructor.
  super->constructor( ).

  description = TEXT-t01.
  category    = me->ci_category.
ENDMETHOD.

This category will later appear in the SCI administration screen and will act as a container for all custom validations.

Creating the Check Class

Next, create the actual validation check by inheriting from CL_CI_TEST_ROOT.

In the constructor, define the basic metadata of the check:

  • Description
  • Category
  • Display position
  • Version
  • Error messages
METHOD constructor.
  super->constructor( ).

  description = `Minimum ABAP Unit Coverage`.
  category    = `Your Custom Category`.
  position    = `010`.
  version    += 1.

  APPEND VALUE #(
           sign   = `I`
           option = `EQ`
           low    = `1PRG`
         ) TO me->typelist.

  APPEND VALUE #(
           test = me->myname
           code = `CI001`
           kind = me->c_error
           text = 'Insufficient coverage: &1% (min. &2%)'
         ) TO me->scimessages.
ENDMETHOD.

Once activated and registered in SCI, the category and the check should appear in the SCI management screen.

New checks

Category and new check

Adding Configuration Parameters

One of the main goals of this implementation was to make the validation configurable.

Instead of hardcoding values, the minimum coverage threshold and object filters are maintained through the SCI variant.

To achieve this, I redefined the method IF_CI_TEST~QUERY_ATTRIBUTES.

This allows us to build a custom parameter screen such as:

  • Minimum Coverage (%)
  • Created After
  • Object Type
  • BAdI Implementations Only
  • RAP Behavior Implementations Only
METHOD if_ci_test~query_attributes.
  DATA(attributes) = VALUE sci_atttab(
    ...
  ).

  DATA(break) =
    cl_ci_query_attributes=>generic(
      p_name       = me->myname
      p_title      = me->description
      p_attributes = attributes
      p_display    = p_display ).
ENDMETHOD.

The resulting configuration screen looks like this:

Screen

Persisting Variant Parameters

The values entered by users need to be stored and restored whenever the variant is executed.

This is done by redefining the methods GET_ATTRIBUTES and PUT_ATTRIBUTES.

METHOD get_attributes.
  EXPORT attributes_filled = attributes_filled
    TO DATA BUFFER p_attributes.
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD put_attributes.
  IMPORT attributes_filled = attributes_filled
    FROM DATA BUFFER p_attributes.
ENDMETHOD.

Implementing the Validation Logic

The heart of every ATC check is the RUN method.

This method is executed for every analyzed object.

METHOD run.
  CHECK me->program_name IS NOT INITIAL.
  CHECK me->get( ) = me->c_true.

  CHECK me->object_type IN me->attributes_filled-object_type.
  CHECK me->is_after_minimum_creation_date( ) >=
        me->attributes_filled-date_from.

  DATA(percentage) = me->get_coverage( ).

  IF percentage < me->attributes_filled-coverage_minimun.

    inform(
      p_sub_obj_type = me->c_type_include
      p_sub_obj_name = me->program_name
      p_kind         = me->c_error
      p_test         = me->myname
      p_code         = `CI001`
      p_param_1      = |{ percentage NUMBER = USER }|
      p_param_2      = |{ me->attributes_filled-coverage_minimun NUMBER = USER }|
    ).
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

Measuring ABAP Unit Coverage

One of the most interesting parts of this implementation was discovering that ABAP Unit coverage can be measured programmatically.

The class CL_AUCV_TASK provides the necessary APIs.

METHOD get_coverage.
  DATA(aunit) =
    cl_aucv_task=>create(
      i_measure_coverage = abap_true ).

  ...

  percentage =
    branch_coverage->get_percentage( ).
ENDMETHOD.

This allows the ATC check to compare the actual coverage with the threshold configured in the SCI variant.

Executing the Check

After creating an SCI variant and selecting the custom check, simply configure the desired threshold.

For example:

  • Created After = 01.01.2025
  • Minimum Coverage = 85%
  • Object Type = CLAS

First, let's measure the ABAP Unit coverage of a sample object:

ABAP Unit

When ATC is executed, findings are generated whenever the object's coverage is below the required percentage.

ATC Result

Lessons Learned

  • ATC is far more extensible than it initially appears.
  • Custom checks can be used to implement real governance requirements.
  • ABAP Unit coverage can be measured programmatically.
  • Configurable checks simplify gradual adoption.
  • Quality gates are an effective way to increase test adoption.

Final Thoughts

By combining the SCI framework, ATC extensibility and ABAP Unit coverage APIs, it is possible to build lightweight but powerful quality controls directly inside the SAP development process.

In addition to ATC execution, I also integrated this validation into the transport release process, ensuring that new developments cannot be released when they fail to meet the required coverage threshold.

Have you ever implemented a custom ATC validation in your landscape? Feel free to share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: Ensuring Quality in BADI Implementations with ABAP Unit
entry.content:
Introduction

In a previous article, I described how to identify and implement the BADI FIN_PROFIT_CENTER_VALIDATION to enforce business rules during Profit Center maintenance.

However, implementing a solution is only part of the job. Once the enhancement is in production, new requirements, bug fixes, and refactoring activities can easily introduce regressions if the validation logic is not properly tested.

This is where ABAP Unit becomes essential. By creating automated tests for enhancement implementations, we can verify business rules consistently and gain confidence when evolving the solution over time.

In this article, I will share a practical example of how I tested a BADI implementation using ABAP Unit based on a real-world validation scenario.

Why Testing a BAdI Matters

BADI implementations often contain critical business logic. In many projects, this logic evolves gradually as new requirements are added. Without automated tests, every change introduces a risk of unexpected side effects.

The validation implemented in FIN_PROFIT_CENTER_VALIDATION ensures that the Segment value remains consistent with the last digit of the Profit Center. Whenever this rule is violated, an error message must be generated and the maintenance process must be blocked.

The business rule is relatively simple:

Last DigitExpected Segment
0GERAL
1ATO
2NAO_ATO

Although the rule itself is straightforward, it is a perfect candidate for automated testing because it contains clearly defined inputs and expected outcomes.

Test Class Design

Before creating individual test cases, I structured the test class to maximize readability and reduce duplication. The objective was to make each test focus only on the business rule being verified.

The class uses standard setup and teardown methods to create and release the class under test. This guarantees that each test executes in isolation and avoids side effects from previous executions.

METHOD setup.
  CREATE OBJECT me->f_cut.
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD teardown.
  FREE me->f_cut.
  REFRESH me->messages.
ENDMETHOD.

The BADI method expects a FIN_ENH_PROFIT_CENTER structure as input and returns validation messages through the CT_MESSAGES parameter. Since several test cases share the same execution flow, I introduced a helper method named ASSERT_NO_VALIDATION_ERROR.

This helper method prepares test data, executes the BADI, handles unexpected runtime exceptions, and verifies that no validation message was raised.

METHOD assert_no_validation_error.
    " Given
    DATA(profit_center_data) = VALUE fin_enh_profit_center( validityenddate	               = `19000101`
                                                            controllingareaforedit         = `SI01`
                                                            profitcenterforedit	           = profitcenter
                                                            validityenddateforedit         = `99991231`
                                                            validitystartdate	             = `20260623`
                                                            profitcentername               = `Z999999999`
                                                            profitctrresponsiblepersonname = `DFARCIC`
                                                            profitcentercreationdate       = `20260623`
                                                            profitcentercreatedbyuser	     = `DFARCIC`
                                                            profitcenterstandardhierarchy	 = `0101`
                                                            segment                        = segment ).

    " When
    TRY.
        me->f_cut->if_badi_fin_pc_validation~execute( EXPORTING is_profit_center = profit_center_data
                                                      CHANGING  ct_messages      = me->messages ).
      CATCH cx_ble_runtime_error INTO DATA(lx_error).
        cl_abap_unit_assert=>fail( msg = lx_error->get_text( ) ).
    ENDTRY.

    " Then
    cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_initial( act = me->messages ).
  ENDMETHOD.

Using a helper method significantly reduced code duplication and allowed the individual test methods to remain concise and focused on their specific scenario.

Implementing the Test Scenario

To validate the implementation comprehensively, I created tests covering three different categories of behavior.

The first category verifies situations where the last digit of the Profit Center is not one of the supported values (0, 1, or 2). In these cases, the validation should simply be ignored.

METHOD ignore_when_last_digit_not_012.
  ...
ENDMETHOD.

The second category focuses on invalid combinations. In the following example, the Profit Center ends with 0, which means the expected Segment should be GERAL. Since the supplied value is ATO, the validation must generate an error message.

METHOD error_when_last_digit_is_0.
    " Given
    DATA(profit_center_data) = VALUE fin_enh_profit_center( validityenddate	               = `19000101`
                                                            controllingareaforedit         = `SI01`
                                                            profitcenterforedit	           = `Z999999990`
                                                            validityenddateforedit         = `99991231`
                                                            validitystartdate	             = `20260623`
                                                            profitcentername               = `Z999999999`
                                                            profitctrresponsiblepersonname = `DFARCIC`
                                                            profitcentercreationdate       = `20260623`
                                                            profitcentercreatedbyuser	     = `DFARCIC`
                                                            profitcenterstandardhierarchy	 = `0101`
                                                            segment                        = `ATO` ).

    " When
    TRY.
        me->f_cut->if_badi_fin_pc_validation~execute( EXPORTING is_profit_center = profit_center_data
                                                      CHANGING  ct_messages      = me->messages ).
      CATCH cx_ble_runtime_error INTO DATA(lx_error).
        cl_abap_unit_assert=>fail( msg = lx_error->get_text( ) ).
    ENDTRY.

    " Then
    DATA(expected_messages) = VALUE fin_enh_pc_message_t( ( msgid = `ZFIN`
                                                            msgty = `E`
                                                            msgno = 001
                                                            msgv1 = `GERAL` ) ).

    cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals( act = me->messages          " Data object with current value
                                        exp = expected_messages ).  " Data object with expected type
  ENDMETHOD.

Finally, positive test cases verify that valid combinations do not generate any validation messages.

METHOD validate_when_last_digit_is_1.

  me->assert_no_validation_error(
    profitcenter = 'Z999999991'
    segment      = 'ATO' ).

ENDMETHOD.
METHOD validate_when_last_digit_is_2.

  me->assert_no_validation_error(
    profitcenter = 'Z999999992'
    segment      = 'NAO_ATO' ).

ENDMETHOD.

Lessons Learned and Clean ABAP Considerations

One interesting aspect of this exercise is how testability influenced the overall design of the solution. The need to create clear and maintainable tests encouraged the use of small methods, descriptive names, and reusable helper methods.

The resulting test class follows several Clean ABAP principles:

  • Small and focused test methods
  • Meaningful and descriptive names
  • Helper methods to eliminate duplication
  • Explicit use of me-> for clarity
  • Minimal shared state between tests

Another takeaway is that even relatively small BADI implementations benefit from automated testing. The effort required to create the tests was modest, while the long-term benefits in maintainability and confidence are substantial.

Final Thoughts

Implementing a BAdI is only the first step. Ensuring that the implementation remains reliable over time is equally important.

ABAP Unit provided a simple and effective way to validate the business rules implemented in FIN_PROFIT_CENTER_VALIDATION while making future changes much safer.

If you are developing custom validations through enhancement spots or BAdIs, I strongly recommend investing a little extra time in automated tests—it pays off quickly.

👉I would be interested to hear how other teams are testing their BAdI implementations and validation frameworks.

entry.title: One RAP Action, Infinite APIs: Mastering RAP Redefined Parameter and Deep Mapping
entry.content:
If you are building APIs in ABAP RESTful Application Programming(RAP) with complex data structures, reusing your code for different systems can be really tough. I recently handled this by implementing RAP Action Parameter Redefinition for a complex business requirement. While the architectural benefits were really good and the development process brought me unexpected SAP kernel bugs and framework behaviours. In this blog, I will walk through the exact development flow, the challenges I ran into, and a solid workaround pattern for mapping deep hierarchical structures without breaking the system. 
 
The Business Case
Consider there is a single RAP BO Action holding a massive and complex material master processing logic. This action handles everything from material headers and plant associations to sales delivery data and error logging.Here the Challenge is such different external systems need to use this exact same logic through the RAP API. However, they do not want or need to send the entire massive payload required by the metadata. 
The catch here is that In RAP Actions, header and header-related parameters are strictly mandatory, while item-level associations remain optional. If a consumer drops a header field from their payload, SAP Gateway throws an error. On top of that, internal SAP technical names (like FirstSalesSpecProductGroup ) mean absolutely nothing to external consumers. They want internal namings as the business use case like Group1. 
 
Solution:
To solve this, we can use a Base Behavior to hold the full, deep structure, and then build multiple Projection Behaviors customized for each specific business scenario. By using Action Parameter Redefinition, we can expose a user specific payload at the projection layer while redirecting all the actual logic back to that single Base implementation class. 
 
Why Redefined Parameters?
  1. Reusability: One base class handles the core logic. Multiple projections handle unique business processes.
  2. Customized I/O: Projections only expose the fields they need.
  3. No Payload Tension: Callers aren't forced to send dummy data for mandatory decimal or date fields they don't use.
  4. Customized Field namings: We can map internal SAP field names to modern, external API-friendly names.

So is Action Parameter Redefining is a part of RAP Extensions?

No, RAP Parameter Redefining does not comes under RAP Extensions directly, since both the methods have distinct limitations. 

RAP Action Parameter redefinition belongs to RAP Business Object (BO) Layering or Consumption with Projection layering. 
While both concepts involve modifying a Business Object, they serve completely different purposes in RAP.
 
Difference
  • Parameter Redefinition (BO Layering): This is a top-down narrowing approach. A wide or complex parameter at the base layer is created and simple/Business specific projection or interface layer is created on top of it to expose a limited field data to a particular UI application or OData service. Here inorder to create redefinition of base, the required fields at projection should first exist in base. If not first base level abstract entity should be extended and respective fields should be added. Post that it can be consumed at Projection/Interface layer.
  • RAP Extensibility (BDEF Extensions): This is a bottom-up expanding approach. This will be used when requirement comes to add new fields, validations etc to standard SAP Business Object without modifying the original code.

So in simple terms if you want to add new fields to existing BDef by standard then go with RAP Extensions and if you want to use limited fields from Base Action to handle another Business scenario then use RAP Parameter Redefinitions. 

Prerequisites

  • So, lets take Material Master standard API - API_PRODUCT as reference. We are gonna recreate same modelling in RAP with Redefined Action Parameters. Note: I will not do each validations and code level reimplementation of Material master standard API here, instead i will perform the same Modelling using RAP.
  • The BASE Layer in our Modelling will be a Consumption CDS View which will have a Behavior Definition which has one ACTION which handles CRUD Operation of Material Master.
  • Why Action ? - We can achieve this through CREATE Method as well. But keep the Fiori app mindset aside and think from Interface perspective. If an third party system API triggers backend SAP System to do MM Activities, they will expect response as well. so Create have Failed/Reported parameters which supports only failure or success pop up kind of OData header response, but it wont support OData body level response and Deep responses. 
  • To achieve this we must use Deep Action. So the BASE Layer should be built on top of consumption view and in Behaviour Definition of consumption view, An Action would be create which will have Deep Input and Response of Material Master which includes all fields. 
  • On top of Base view, First Projection view will be created and for our business use case lets consider - Business Scenario-1 is trying to reuse the Material Master Base API's Action by using redefined parameters with limited field from base. ( i.e. in OData based approach we generally do OData redefinition / extension for such use case. but still it has its own limitations of standard validations over fields etc. But with the custom RAP Approach, its complete dynamic design and end user would have control over everything ). 
  • On top of Base view Second Projection view will be created again for Business scenario -2 . 
  • Both Business scenario 1 and 2 will try to reuse limited fields from BASE for their use case with their respective namings for input and response payload.
  • All the Base, Business scenario-1 & 2 actions parameters should have respective abstract behaviour definitions and mapping should be done at each level redirecting to BASE Behaviour definition. 

Design Architecture:

Please go through this flow chart carefully which explains the complete design architecture for our implementation.

Lets start development...!

BASE LAYER - GENERIC COMPLETE PAYLOAD

1. The CDS Consumption view ZC_MATERIAL_MASTER_GENERIC is created with exposure of only one key field. Since our business logic is packed in RAP Action, This layer acts as dummy layer which helps to create behaviour definition on top of it.  

Note: Whatever artifacts are created, please use the term extensible wherever possible, so that other business user can able to extend your artifacts and add additional fields if required. This is the practice followed for dynamic API approach. 

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Material Master Base view'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@VDM.viewType: #CONSUMPTION
@AbapCatalog.extensibility.extensible: true
define root view entity ZC_MATERIAL_MASTER_GENERIC as select from A_Product

2. The Behaviour Definition for Consumption view ZC_MATERIAL_MASTER_GENERIC is created on top of CDS View. In the consumption view Deep Action is defined. 

unmanaged implementation in class zcl_material_master_base unique;
strict ( 2 );
extensible;
define behavior for ZC_MATERIAL_MASTER_GENERIC alias MaterialAPI
lock master
authorization master ( instance ) extensible
{
  action   l_material_api  deep parameter ZA_MATERIAL_API_PARAMETER deep result [0..*] ZA_MATERIAL_API_PARAMETER;
  create;
  field ( readonly ) Material;
}

3. Now let's start with Abstract Entity creation for Material Master. Since Material Master uses API_PRODUCT standard API, We will take reference of the same. API_PRODUCT constructs payload from SADL CDS Reference A_PRODUCT. From A_PRODUCT multiple deep structure goes to multiple view components of MM. Like Basic view, Plant view etc. As part of this blog we are not going to replicate complete MM. If we do so then blog will go very lengthy. so the aim is to expose large set of data in Base view from Material master and use some limited data from those large set in Projection layer redefinitions.

  • Now we have all abstract entities ready for PROJECTION layer. Let's build a final Abstract Behaviour Definition for the Root Abstract Entity.
  • Abstract Behaviour Definition for ZA_MAT_PARAM_BS1 is created and here the associations on each layer should be exposed correctly as below. 
  • Here comes the important part which is MAPPING. Compared to BASE level, we have not considered many fields in PROJECTION-1 for BS-1 and we renamed some fields at SalesDelivery level and Log level based on BS-1 Requirements. To ensure the seamless flow of data happens without any error, we should do mapping at PROJECTION ABSTRACT BDEF level redirecting to BASE ABSTRACT BDEF. 
abstract;
strict ( 2 );
with hierarchy;
define behavior for za_mat_param_bs1
{
  association _MaterialData;
  association _log;
  deep mapping for za_material_api_parameter corresponding  {
      Id      = Id;
      Product = Product;
      AckCode = AckCode;
      Status  = Status;
      sub _MaterialData = _MaterialData;
      sub _log = _log;
    }
}

define behavior for za_bs1_error_log
{
  deep mapping for za_material_error_log corresponding
    {
      Product   = Product;
      ErrorCode = MessageCode;
      ErrorMsg  = Message;
    }
}


define behavior for za_material_bs1_input
{
  association _Plant;
  association _SalesDelivery;
  deep mapping for za_material_base_input corresponding
    {
      Product = Product;
      sub _Plant = _Plant;
      sub _SalesDelivery = _SalesDelivery;
    }
}

define behavior for za_bs1_product_plant
{
  deep mapping for za_product_plant corresponding
    {
      Product = Product;
      Plant   = Plant;
    }
}

define behavior for za_bs1_product_sales_dlv
{
  deep mapping for za_product_sales_delivery corresponding
    {
      Product                 = Product;
      ProductSalesOrg         = ProductSalesOrg;
      ProductDistributionChnl = ProductDistributionChnl;
      Group1                  = FirstSalesSpecProductGroup;
    }
}

Major things to notice in PROJECTION-1 Abstract entity BDef:

  • Here mapping is done at each association level redirecting to parent entity. This mapping should be done manually and it wont be autogenerated. 
  • The renamed Group1, ErrorCode, ErrMsg is correctly mapped to base target fields.
  • Same like fields, associations also should be mapped using the syntax "SUB" . "CORRESPONDING" is mandatory to make sure associations are set perfectly at each level.

Henceforth, in this way RAP Action Parameter Redefinition is used to decouple Material Master API at base and projection layer. Not only Material Master API for interface, but also this approach can use used for Fiori app integrations as well based on the requirement. Moreover, I can say this is a very good feature given by RAP to use Mandatory Action Parameter based on business requirement. This makes the backend highly reusable and reliable.  Also, OData V4 on top of this makes the metadata lighter and powerful.

entry.title: EWM Pick Label Printing: Confirmed WT, Serial Numbers & Destination bin on the label
entry.content:
Introduction

I wanted to print a WO picking label automatically after confirming a warehouse task in RF.  Among the fields I wanted to have on the label were the WT number, destination bin, and serial numbers. I want to share my findings and how I approached this case.

How Standard WO Printing Works

When a warehouse order triggers a PPF print action, the call goes through several layers. The entry point is the PPF action class /SCWM/CL_IM_WOSINGLE, which simply delegates to the common execution FM:

METHOD if_ex_exec_methodcall_ppf~execute.
* Processing method for printing single document for
*   warehouse order. Print one TO per document page.
* Prefered SmartForms is /SCWM/WO_SINGLE

* Call of common function module for execution
*   for all PPF action definitions for WO printing
    CALL FUNCTION '/SCWM/EXECUTE_PPF_WO'
      EXPORTING
        flt_val             = flt_val
        io_appl_object      = io_appl_object
        ...
ENDMETHOD.

From there, using /SCWM/EXECUTE_PPF_WO_PDF as an example (other variants exist depending on the form type), the call stack looks like this:

PPF trigger
  -> /SCWM/EXECUTE_PPF_WO        (printer determination, data collection)
    -> /SCWM/EXECUTE_PPF_WO_PDF  (form routing, data preparation - PDF variant as example)
      -> FORM initlization        (this is where the decision happens)
        -> Adobe Form

Two internal tables carry WT data through this flow:

  • lt_ordim_o - open warehouse tasks
  • lt_ordim_c - confirmed warehouse tasks

Both get populated and passed down. Which one ends up in the form is decided in FORM initlization.

The Core Problem

Inside FORM initlization in include /SCWM/LPRINTINGPDF, there's this block. SAP's comment says "on re-print" but the actual condition is just whether ORDIM_O is empty or not - it doesn't know or care about the context:

* On re-print we don't have data in ORDIM_O.
* Only ORDIM_C is filled. The document is based on
* data from ORDIM_O. Therefor we must fill ORDIM_O
* with ORDIM_C data.

IF p_gt_ordim_o[] IS INITIAL.
    LOOP AT p_gt_ordim_c INTO ls_ordim_c.
        MOVE-CORRESPONDING ls_ordim_c TO ls_ordim_o.
        MOVE ls_ordim_c-nistm TO ls_ordim_o-vsolm.
        MOVE ls_ordim_c-nista TO ls_ordim_o-vsola.
        MOVE ls_ordim_c-tapos TO ls_ordim_o-noitm.
        APPEND ls_ordim_o TO p_gt_wordim_o.
    ENDLOOP.
ELSE.
    LOOP AT p_gt_ordim_o INTO ls_ordim_o.
        APPEND ls_ordim_o TO p_gt_wordim_o.
    ENDLOOP.
ENDIF.

The logic:

  • Open WTs exist - print those, ignore confirmed completely
  • No open WTs - fall back to confirmed WTs

The form always reads from p_gt_wordim_o. Confirmed tasks only get there if ORDIM_O is empty.

What Happens in Practice

Say a warehouse order has 50 tasks.

Trigger on WO creation - all 50 WTs are open, lt_ordim_o has 50 entries, prints fine.

Trigger on WT 1 confirmation - WT 1 moves to lt_ordim_c, WTs 2-50 are still in lt_ordim_o. Since lt_ordim_o is not empty, the ELSE branch runs. WTs 2-50 print. WT 1, the one just confirmed, is ignored.

Reprint after all WTs confirmed - lt_ordim_o is empty, the IF branch kicks in, the confirmed WT gets mapped across, and it prints correctly.

 

Scenario lt_ordim_o lt_ordim_cWhat prints
Print on WO creation50 open WTsemptyAll 50 open WTs
Print on WT 1 confirmationWTs 2-50WT 1WTs 2-50 (WT 1 ignored)
Reprint after all confirmedempty1 confirmed WTThat confirmed WT

This is by design. The form was built around open WTs, with confirmed as a fallback for reprint. It's just not built for mid-sequence confirmation printing.

What SAP Gives You as a Hook

For standard form names the CASE statement hardcodes the call to initlization directly:

WHEN '/SCWM/WO_SINGLE' OR '/SCWM/WO_MULTIPLE'.
    lt_ordim_c  = it_ordim_c.
    lt_ordim_cs = it_ordim_cs.

    PERFORM initlization USING is_doc_params
                               it_ordim_o
                               it_ordim_c
                               ...

For custom form names the code falls into WHEN OTHERS and a BAdI fires:

WHEN OTHERS.
    TRY.
        GET BADI lo_badi FILTERS lgnum = iv_lgnum.
    CATCH cx_badi.
        MESSAGE e081(/scwm/print) WITH iv_form_name INTO lv_text.
        ev_status = '2'.
        RAISE error.
    ENDTRY.
    IF lo_badi IS BOUND.
        CALL BADI lo_badi->get_add_wo_data
          EXPORTING
            is_who      = is_who
            it_ordim_o  = lt_ordim_o
            it_ordim_c  = lt_ordim_c
          IMPORTING
            et_oridm_o  = lt_ordim_o
            et_ordim_c  = lt_ordim_c.
    ENDIF.

So if you copy the standard form to a custom name and implement BAdI /SCWM/EX_PRNT_PDF_WO, you get full control over what goes into lt_ordim_o before initlization runs. You could for example simply clear lt_ordim_o, which would force the IF branch to run and map the confirmed WTs from lt_ordim_c instead. That solves the open WT problem.

But there are two more issues. First, ORDIM_C at that point contains all previously confirmed WTs in the WO, not just the current one. You'd still need logic to identify which specific WT was just confirmed. Second, PPF fires during or immediately after confirmation and the confirmation may not yet be committed to the database at that point. So even the data you're trying to read might not be there yet.

Interestingly, SAP themselves documented this complexity right in the code comments of FORM initlization that was already mentioned above:

* On re-print it could be that we have more than one
* ORDIM_C data. Field NOITM contains TAPOS!
* Serialnumber handling: Depending on open or confirmed WTs
*  On confirmed WTs only read serial numbers from ORDIM_CS and fill
*    WT_ORDIM_CS
*  On open WTs check if ORDIM_OS has entries. If yes, move them to
*    WT_ORDIM_CS (and add ___ for partial predefinition). If no, check
*    serial number profile. On 'C' fill WT_ORDIM_CS with ___.

SAP knew that ORDIM_C can have multiple entries and that you'd need TAPOS/NOITM to identify individual WTs. They also knew that serial numbers for open WTs are just placeholders. If you want the actual confirmed serial numbers on the label, you need confirmed WTs - which means you're back to the same problem. The PPF approach has known limitations even from SAP's perspective. It gets complicated fast.

Why Not Print from the RF Dialog?

Triggering the print directly from the RF PAI function module was also considered. The timing would be fine since the WT data is in memory right there.

The problem was serial numbers. The requirement is to have serial numbers on the label, and serial number capture in RF happens on a separate screen with its own PAI FM. That would have meant hooking into two different places and coordinating between them, which adds complexity without a good reason when a cleaner option exists.

The Fix: BAdI /SCWM/EX_CORE_CO_POST

There is a BAdI /SCWM/EX_CORE_CO_POST from Enhancement Spot /SCWM/ES_CORE_CO, described as Posting of Confirmed Warehouse Tasks.

This BAdI fires after the confirmation is fully posted and committed. By the time the implementation runs, IT_ORDIM_C has the confirmed WT, IT_ORDIM_CS has the serial numbers, and there's no timing risk. Everything arrives together in one shot. No need to identify the right WT from a list, no timing uncertainty, no coordination between multiple PAI FMs.

CALL BADI lo_badi->post
  EXPORTING
    iv_lgnum       = iv_lgnum
    it_ordim_c     = it_ordim_c     " confirmed WTs, already committed
    it_ordim_cs    = it_ordim_cs    " confirmed serial numbers
    it_ltap_vb     = it_tap         " original planned destination bin
    ...

The implementation opens an FP job, calls the Adobe Form with ORDIM_C and ORDIM_CS, and closes the job. No separate data collection class needed.

One thing to keep in mind: this BAdI fires on every WT posting across the whole system, not just picking. The filters need to be tight. At minimum filter on LGNUM, warehouse process types, and source / destination storage types, otherwise you'll end up printing a label for every single WT confirmation in the warehouse regardless of the process.

The Destination Bin Problem

The label also must show the destination bin. At the moment of confirmation, ORDIM_C-NLPLA doesn't contain the bin. It contains the resource, because SAP overwrites the planned destination with the resource when the task gets assigned to a picker.

I found out though, that original planned destination is available in IT_LTAP_VB, which is passed to the BAdI. Read it from there and pass it to the form. The data is there, just not where you'd expect it to be.

The Downside: No Built-in Reprint

Going with the POST BAdI instead of PPF means losing the reprint functionality that PPF provides out of the box. With PPF you can trigger a reprint from the warehouse monitor through the standard action framework. With the POST BAdI there's no equivalent. The BAdI fires once at posting time and that's it.

The fallback is SP01. The spool request from the original print stays there and can be reprinted from there. It works but it's not user friendly since you need to search by date, user, or spool number to find the right entry.

A proper reprint option would need a custom button in the warehouse monitor and a custom FM that reads ORDIM_C and ORDIM_CS by TANUM and calls the same print logic. Doable, but it's additional effort.

Summary

Standard EWM WO printing always prioritises open tasks. The confirmed WT only makes it to the form when no open tasks are left. For confirmation-time label printing where you need the WT number, destination bin, and serial numbers, PPF might be tricky. BAdI /SCWM/EX_CORE_CO_POST solves the data problem, the timing problem, and the serial number coordination in one go. The tradeoff is that reprint requires extra work.

If you ran into this and found a different approach or spotted a gap in what I described here, would be good to hear it in the comments!

entry.title: Automated custom code adaptation for SAP S/4HANA and SAP HANA on your SAP ECC system
entry.content:
In the preparation phase of your custom code migration process from SAP ECC system to SAP S/4HANA you execute S/4HANA readiness checks using the Custom Code Migration app (see also Custom code analysis for SAP S/4HANA with SAP Fiori App Custom Code Migration)  and get a long list of S/4HANA related issues in your custom code, which must be solved during S/4HANA system conversion.

Among them there are also such issues like for example usage in your custom code of no longer available in S/4HANA SAP standard data elements or other Data Dictionary objects. After you convert your system to S/4HANA such issues will result in syntax errors. The situation becomes even more critical if you use the removed standard Data Dictionary objects in your custom Data Dictionary objects, since during system conversion Software Update Manager (SUM) will activate all Data Dictionary objects and this will result in syntax errors, which you would need to solve without any tool support.

Besides this there are also other use cases like for example missing ORDER BY in SELECT statements, which bring up a lot of issues in your custom code but are pure technical adjustments which can be solved in advance on your ECC system thereby minimizing the required post-conversion remediation on the converted S/4HANA system. The automated resolution of these technical findings will be equally valuable for pure SAP HANA migrations, reducing manual effort and accelerating the migration process.

This blog post describes how such issues can be resolved in automated way on your ECC system using so-called transferable quick fixes to reduce your adaptation efforts after S/4HANA system conversion or during SAP HANA migration.

If you want to get a preview how ECC quick fixes work directly in the system environment watch the following YouTube video.

PLEASE NOTE: For usage and download of ECC quick fixes in the Custom Code Migration app you do not need access to Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities. It is only required if you want to use Code Explain or ATC Explain in the Custom Code Migration app (as shown in the video).

Prerequisites

The Custom Code Migration app is set up on your SAP BTP ABAP environment and connected via RFC and SAP Cloud Connector to your on-prem ECC system.

The SAP note 3756014 - Mass Quick Fix Application in ATC must implemented in your on-prem ECC system. Please follow exactly and execute all manual activities provided in the SAP note.

For technical setup instructions for the Custom Code Migration app in SAP BTP ABAP environment please refer to the blog post ABAP custom code analysis using SAP Business Technology Platform and also check the SAP Discovery Center mission Use SAP Fiori Custom Code Migration App to Analyze Your ABAP Custom Code for SAP S/4HANA Readiness.

How to apply quick fixes on your SAP ECC system

After execution of custom code analysis for S/4HANA in the Custom Code Migration app (“SAP S/4HANA Migration Project”) you will get a list with ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) findings. If you have set up SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities for your SAP BTP ABAP environment and enabled AI-based features in the Custom Code Migration app, then by using the AI-based explain on the finding for example for usage of removed data element FILE you would see that the recommendation to resolve it on the ECC system before system conversion is already proposed by AI in the explanation of the issue. The proposed resolution to create a copy of the FILE data element in your custom code, is also possible only on your ECC system, because on the S/4HANA system the FILE data element does not exist anymore.

The new filter Transferable Quick Fix in the Custom Code Migration app allows you to display ATC findings which can be adjusted with quick fixes on your ECC system.

You can download the ATC findings, which can be resolved automatically with transferable quick fixes on your ECC system from the Findings list into ZIP file by using the menu Export Table ->Export Transferable Quick Fixes.

After that open the SAP GUI transaction ATC in your ECC system and double click Upload and Run ATC Quick Fixes.

Here you first click Upload Quick Fixes to upload the ZIP file with your downloaded ATC findings for adaptation with transferable quick fixes. Then provide your packages where the copies of removed standard data elements will be created as custom data elements and Run Quick Fixes. Finally Activate the changes, and you are done.

In this example transferable quick fixes created the custom data element ZFILE5 in the custom code package and replaced with them usages of standard FILE data element, which was removed in S/4HANA.

If you now go back to your Custom Code Migration project and Start Analysis Run again, you will see that the overall amount of your findings was reduced because of the issues, which were solved by applying the transferable quick fixes on your ECC system.

Transferable quick fixes are currently available for removed data elements and for missing ORDER BY in SELECT statements. Just try them out!

entry.title: An introduction to agent skills for ABAP development with GitHub Copilot
entry.content:
Introduction

When working with AI for ABAP development, one of the first things that we encounter is that the outcome of the AI is not always aligned with the result that we expect unless detailed context and instructions are provided. In order to avoid giving the same information repeatedly with every prompt, or bloating the context of the AI with lengthy instructions that are only relevant for specific cases, we can use agent skills. These can be seen as context or instructions "on-demand" that are only loaded and applied when required.

 

What is an agent skill?

This section is a brief summary of the information that can be found in https://agentskills.io/home . From this, an agent skill is defined as "a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows.". Basically, it is a folder that contains a SKILL.md file that defines the skill, along with a structure of different directories with resources that can be used by the agent. A typical skill structure is then as follows:

skill-name/
├── SKILL.md          # Required file: metadata + instructions
├── scripts/          # Optional directory: contains executable code
├── references/       # Optional directory: contains documentation
├── assets/           # Optional directory: contains templates, resources
└── ...               # Any additional files or directories

SKILL.md file

This is the key element. It is a text file that has a YAML frontmatter (metadata enclosed between '---')  followed by markdown instructions (skill instructions). This frontmatter has two mandatory properties:

  • name: it is the name of the skill. Should be equal to the folder name where the skill is located, and must be 1-64 characters containing Unicode lowercase alphanumeric characters (a-z, 0-9) and hyphens (-). 
  • description: as we will discuss later, this is the relevant part. It describes what the skill does and when to use it. It must be 1-1024 characters.

After the YAML frontmatter comes the skill instructions (Body content) in markdown format. In this case there are no format restrictions or specifications. It is recommended to include step-by-step instructions, examples and common edge cases. It is recommended that the skill does not exceed 500 lines.

A simple example of a skill is as follows:

---
name: friendly-greeting
description: Use this skill whenever the user says hello or good morning to provide an upbeat response and a random joke.
---

When the user greets you:
1. Reply with an enthusiastic "Hello there! Ready to build something great today?"
2. Share one short, clean programming or tech joke.
3. Ask how you can assist with their current project.

Optional directories

Along with the skill definition and instructions, we can include additional information in specific folders. The following ones are the convention that is usually used:

  • scripts/: contains executable code for the agent.
  • references/: contains additional documentation
  • assets/: contains static resources (templates, images, data files)

All the files contained in these directories should be referenced in the skill using relative paths from the skill root. For example: "See [the reference guide](references/REFERENCE.md) for details."

Progressive disclosure

This is the key property of the skill. AI Agents load skill information progressively, allowing efficient use of the context:

  • At startup, AI agents load only the name and description of all the Skills (the YAML frontmatter).
  • When the AI agent decides that the skill is required, it will load all the skill instructions and use it in the context. This is the reason why a good description is a critical point. It will ensure that the skill is used only when needed, keeping the context clean of information not relevant for the process.
  • Only when the agent detects that one of the skill's resources is required (scripts, references, assets, etc...) then is it loaded.

How to use skills in Eclipse with GitHub Copilot

To use skills in Eclipse with the GitHub Copilot plugin we have two main options. The first one (project-scoped skill) is to include, apart from the ABAP Projects that we have configured for the different systems, a General Project with a .github or .claude or .agents directory within it (I use .github). Within this directory, the skills must be located in a skills subdirectory. GitHub Copilot will then include all the skills defined in this directory even if you are working with other ABAP Projects (I think this is counterintutive, but this is how it works).

As reference we can review the setup that was used in the example of this blog. In this case I have a folder called abap-ai-skills, that contains the two skills that will be discussed later:

One simple procedure to generate this setup is to create the skills in a specific folder of the PC, and afterwards, from Eclipse, generate the project with File->Import->General->Projects from Folder or Archive.

Another option is to use a user-scoped skill. In this case the skills files should be placed in the user directory of the PC (C:\Users\<your user name>) and within this directory, in ~/.copilot/skills/<skill-name>/, ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/ or ~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/.

How to use skills in VS Code with GitHub Copilot

To use skills in VS Code we can also choose between two different types of skills:

  • Project-scoped skills: these skills are linked to each repository, and can be located in different directories: .github/skills/, .claude/skills or .agents/skills.
  • User-scoped skills: these skills are stored in your user profile. Their location can be ~/.copilot/skills/, ~/.claude/skills/ or ~/.agents/skills/.

To write this blog I also tested the execution with VS Code, using Project-scoped skill. For this, I re-used the folder that I employed for Eclipse, and I added it to my Workspace:

I have to warn that I am not an expert in VS Code, so maybe this is not the best setup, but this worked for me.

 

ABAP Unit Test Example skills

When working with AI-generated ABAP Unit tests I came across some difficulties:

  • When I have database dependencies, the standard ABAP Test Double Framework was not always applied.
  • I prefer to avoid magic numbers in the tests and give meaningful names as CV_ANY_CUSTOMER to indicate that the value used is not a key element of the process.

Although some models such as Claude Opus 4.7 usually generate pretty good test avoiding the previous mistakes, I would like to have a more consistent outcome using different models. With this in mind I generated two skills:

  • abap-unit-test-doubles: guidelines to use ABAP Test Double Framework (OSQL and Function Modules)
  • abap-unit-test-guidelines: general guidelines to generate ABAP Unit Tests

abap-unit-test-doubles skill

This skills instructs the agent of how to use the Test Double Frameworks for SQL and Function Modules. It contains the following elements:

  • SKILL.md: this is the skill definition file. It will be shown later.
  • .references/test-osql.abap: this file contains an example of SQL Test Double. It contains the Unit Test Include of the standard demo class CL_OSQL_COMPREHENSIVE_DEMO. 
  • .references/test-ftd.abap: this file contains an example of Function Module Test Doubles. It contains the Unit Test Include of the standard demo class CL_FTD_EXPENSE_MANAGER.

The skill file content is:

---
name: abap-unit-test-doubles
description: This document defines how to use Test doubles for ABAP Unit testing when code under test (CUT) has external dependencies (Database or function modules).
---

# ABAP Test Double Framework Use

## Overview

This skills helps me to create proper test doubles using standard test double framework when CUT has database or function module dependencies

## Instructions

### Case 1: Open SQL Test Double Framework (OSQL)
* **Trigger:** CUT performs database operations (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `MODIFY`, `DELETE`) or queries CDS Views.
* ** Generation instructions:**
1. **Key Framework APIs:**
	* Setup: `cl_osql_test_environment=>create( i_dependency_list = VALUE #( ( 'table_or_cds' ) ) )`
	* Insert Mock Data: `environment->insert_test_data( it_data )`
	* Teardown: `environment->destroy( )` / Clear: `environment->clear_doubles( )`
2. **Example reference:** In case you need examples, you can use as technical blueprint reference file `./references/test-osql.abap`.

### Case 2: Function Test Double Framework (FTD)
* **Trigger:** CUT executes `CALL FUNCTION`.
* ** Generation instructions:**
1. **Key Framework APIs:**
  * Setup: `cl_function_test_environment=>create( VALUE #( ( 'FM_NAME' ) ) )`
  * Double Config: `function_test_environment->get_double( 'FM_NAME' )`
  * Behavior: `configure_call( )->when( input_config )->then_set_output( output_config )`
  * Clear: `function_test_environment->clear_doubles( )`
2. **Example reference:** In case you need examples, you can use as technical blueprint reference file `./references/test-ftd.abap`.

abap-unit-test-guidelines skill

This skills instructs the agent of my preferences of ABAP Unit Test generation. It contains only a SKILL.md file with the following content:

---
name: abap-unit-test-guidelines
description: This document defines the guidelines for writing ABAP Unit Tests in the project. Use it when you want to create a new ABAP Unit Test or improve an existing one.
---

# ABAP Unit Test Guidelines

## Overview

This skill helps me to write ABAP Unit Tests in a consistent way across the project. It provides guidelines for writing unit tests, including naming conventions, test structure, and best practices.

## Instructions

### Rule 1: Naming conventions
* **Rule:** 
	* Use LTC_<class test name> for local test classes.
	* Use LTD_<class test double name> for local test doubles classes
	* Use LTH_<class test helper class> for local test helper classes

### Rule 2: Avoid Magic Numbers and Strings in Unit Tests
* **Rule:** You are creating auxiliary variables in your unit test for representing test data. Give these variables meaningful names. For example, you are creating a variable for a test customer and the customer code is not relevant and any can be used, name variable as CV_ANY_CUSTOMER or LV_ANY_CUSTOMER (CV_ is used for constants and LV_ for local variables). Another example would be CV_ANY_OTHER_CUSTOMER if two customers are required for the process.

### Rule 3: Consider the maximum length of test method names
* **Rule:** test method names should have at most 30 characters. Include a comment in method definition previous to method name with a summary of the test intent. Example:
    "Test creation of a travel with no bookings or supplements
    METHODS tc_create_100_ok FOR TESTING.

### Rule 4: Activate objects before executing unit tests
* **Rule:** Before executing unit test always activate CUT and test include.

As can be seen, rule 2 avoids using literals and constants in the test, that was one of my concerns when reviewing unit test generated by AI. Rule 3 and 4 seem a little bit strange, as they are more or less known ABAP rules. However, during my test of the Skill, I often found the AI struggling with errors due to long names for test methods (usually these method names try to include the given-when-then structure), or trying to execute unit test with SAP ADT MCP before activating the class. 

Example execution in Eclipse

To test these skills I copied the standard flight model API /dmo/cl_flight_legacy to a new class (zcl_demo_skills_csn), deleting the existing unit tests. Then I switchted to Agent mode in GitHub Copilot Plugin and asked the Agent several times with different models the same prompt: "Generate Unit test for method create_travel of class ZCL_DEMO_SKILLS_CSN. Consider different cardinalities for Travel, Booking and Booking Suplement. Consider also error cases". What follows is the execution log of one of the runs (in this was executed with "Auto" model):

As can be seen, both skills were loaded, and in this execution the agent also load the reference class for OSQL doubles (notice that it did not load the reference class for function module doubles, as it determined correctly that was not required). It has to be noted during my test that is was not always the case. The skills were always loaded, but the reference files were sometimes not checked. This is due to the fact of the non-deterministic nature of AI agents, sometimes it decided that the reference file is required and in other runs it was fine with the instructions included in the skill.

It is not shown in the log, but it kept thinking for a while, and afterwards implemented the test. Then, as can be seen in the previous image, it asked for permission to execute SAP ADT MCP tool to activate the class (as was also instructed in the skill). I allowed it and the process continued (notice that we can configure the auto-approval of these operations).

As can be seen, after the class is activated, the agent tries to excute unit test with ADT MCP tool also. I allowed it also.

From the previous image, it can be seen that all the tests passed and a summary of the process is shown. I include the source code for the definition part of the test class generated:

*"* use this source file for your ABAP unit test classes

CLASS ltc_create_travel DEFINITION
  FOR TESTING
  RISK LEVEL HARMLESS
  DURATION SHORT.

  PRIVATE SECTION.

    CONSTANTS:
      cv_any_agency_id       TYPE /dmo/agency_id     VALUE '070006',
      cv_any_customer_id     TYPE /dmo/customer_id   VALUE '000001',
      cv_any_currency_eur    TYPE /dmo/currency_code VALUE 'EUR',
      cv_any_currency_usd    TYPE /dmo/currency_code VALUE 'USD',
      cv_any_carrier_id      TYPE /dmo/carrier_id    VALUE 'AA',
      cv_any_connection_id   TYPE /dmo/connection_id VALUE '0017',
      cv_any_carrier_id_2    TYPE /dmo/carrier_id    VALUE 'LH',
      cv_any_connection_id_2 TYPE /dmo/connection_id VALUE '0400',
      cv_any_flight_date     TYPE /dmo/flight_date   VALUE '20991231',
      cv_any_begin_date      TYPE /dmo/begin_date    VALUE '20991201',
      cv_any_end_date        TYPE /dmo/end_date      VALUE '20991231',
      cv_any_booking_date    TYPE /dmo/booking_date  VALUE '20991201',
      cv_any_suppl_id_1      TYPE /dmo/supplement_id VALUE 'SU01',
      cv_any_suppl_id_2      TYPE /dmo/supplement_id VALUE 'SU02',
      cv_bad_agency_id       TYPE /dmo/agency_id     VALUE '999999',
      cv_bad_customer_id     TYPE /dmo/customer_id   VALUE '999999',

    CLASS-DATA environment TYPE REF TO if_osql_test_environment.

      class_setup,

      setup,

This class fulfills the requirements described in the two skills:

  • Name is LTC_<test class name>
  • It uses the ABAP Open SQL Test Double Framework.
  • It has defined meaningful constants for the use in the test.
  • All the tests have a description with the test intent.

Conclusions

In this blog we have discussed AI skills and how they can help us to obtain better outcomes from AI Agents. From my experience, I will suggest to follow these rules:

  • Start small: define skills for things that you notice that the AI agents have difficulties with. If you use AI to generate the skill, review it carefully, as I have found that it usually includes general and not relevant information.
  • Test the skills: check if the skill is used when expected and not taken into account when is not required. Review the description (too general? too specific?) if the skill does not get used as expected.
  • Review the best practices section that you can find in https://agentskills.io/home

For example, consider a Product Management application where all users can display product information, but only users assigned to an Approval/Manager role should be allowed to perform the Manage Status action. 

Requirement would be: 

  • Normal users can display and maintain product data according to their authorization. 
  • Authorized users can execute the Manage Status action.

Output

Login with another user so action is disabled
