entry.title: ATC Table Attributes Check: six things I learned reading the code (and running it on two systems)
entry.content:
Introduction

Every time I open the ATC results of a custom development, there is a block of findings that people scroll past: the ones on database tables. "Buffering is initial", "Change log active", "Buffering permitted but switched off". Most teams either exempt them all or ignore them all.

After answering a question about one of these messages, I got curious about the whole check. So I read the class behind it, in two lab systems, S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755) and S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758), and then ran ATC on real tables of both systems to see each rule fire. The rules and the results below come from the code and from those runs. I didn't create or change anything.

The setup

The check is called "Table Attributes Check" and the class is CL_CI_TEST_DDIC_TABLES. It reads the technical settings of the table (data class, size category, buffering, log changes) plus the delivery class and the fields, and compares them with a list of rules.

In the 2023 system the class registers 43 messages. In both releases the rules I checked have the same conditions and the same priorities, so nothing here depends on the release.

I ran ATC with the default variant of each system on 12 tables: 7 in 2023 and 5 in 2020.

Thing 1: it goes from a note to an error, and the priority is in the code

Most messages of this check are information (priority 3), so they're easy to ignore. But not all of them. From the constructor of the class:

message when priority

0022change log on, data class APPL0 or APPL11 (error)
0023change log on, size category greater than 21 (error)
0137FLOAT field in the primary key1 (error)
0003buffering "allowed but switched off", size category 0 or 12 (warning)
0060more than 3 STRING/RAWSTRING fields2 (warning)
0010, 0013buffering not switched on, delivery class C/G/E/S or data class APPL23
0004buffering "allowed but switched off", size category 2 or more3

So if you filter ATC by priority 1 and 2 only, some of these still show up, and they deserve a look.

Thing 2: change log on master or transaction data is an error

chk_protocol checks the "Log Changes" flag. If it's on and the data class is APPL0 (master data) or APPL1 (transaction data), you get 0022 with priority 1. If the data class is something else but the size category is bigger than 2, you get 0023, also priority 1.

In my runs, ZDEPTO (APPL0) and YTAB_CURSO_BA_AN (APPL0) in 2023, and ZDEMO_DATA (APPL1) in 2020, all got the priority 1 finding. ZARTH_SOL_C in 2020 also has log changes on, but it's a small APPL2 table, and it came back with no finding from this check.

The idea is simple: table logging writes a log record for every change, which makes sense for small customizing tables and not for tables that grow with the business.

Thing 3: "Buffering not allowed" doesn't make the buffering message go away

chk_bufoffdelc fires when the buffering state is anything other than "Buffering switched on" and the delivery class is C, G, E or S. It doesn't matter if the state is "Buffering not allowed" or "allowed but switched off": both fire 0010.

And if the data class is APPL2, chk_bufoffappl adds 0013 with the same condition.

That's exactly what I saw: ZTABELA01 and ZTABELA002 in 2023 and ZTI_HD_CATEG in 2020 (class C, APPL2, "not allowed") got 0010 and 0013. ZTI_HD_CATEGT in 2020 (class C, but APPL0) got only 0010.

So for a small customizing table, the way out is to switch buffering on and choose a type. If you switch it on without a type, chk_bufontype gives you 0015 instead.

Thing 4: a small table that "could be buffered" gets a harder message than a big one

This one surprised me. chk_bufallow_a handles the state "Buffering allowed but switched off":

  • size category 0 or 1: message 0003, priority 2 (warning)
  • size category 2 or more: message 0004, priority 3

So the check is stricter with the small table. It makes sense when you think about it: a small table that is allowed to be buffered and isn't is losing performance for nothing, while for a big table keeping it off is a reasonable choice.

My runs matched both sides: ZCEP (2023) and ZDATAGEN_PROCURE (2020), both size category 0, got the priority 2 warning. YTAB_CURSO_BA_AN (size 4) and ZDEMO_DATA (size 😎 got only the priority 3 note.

Thing 5: strings, FLOAT keys and wide tables

  • More than 3 STRING or RAWSTRING fields give 0060 (warning), except for buffered tables with size category 0. Exactly 3 is fine: ZMARVELCOMIC has 3 STRING fields and came back clean.
  • A FLOAT field in the primary key is 0137, priority 1. The same field in a secondary index is 0037, only a warning.
  • More than 700 fields gives 0021. More than 100 fields is registered as 0020, but with "no message", so you'll never see it.

For these I didn't find a table in my labs that falls in the rule (except the 3-strings limit), so they come from the code only.

Thing 6: almost every message here can be exempted

41 of the 43 messages are registered with the exemption type "by table entry". The two that can't be exempted are the dictionary inconsistency ones (an index field that isn't in the table, a referenced table or view that doesn't exist), which makes sense: those are broken objects, not design choices.

So when a setting is on purpose (a big customizing table you don't want buffered, for example), the clean way is an ATC exemption with the reason, not switching the check off in the variant, which would hide it for every table.

A quick checklist

what you see where to change fix

change log on APPL0/APPL1 (priority 1)technical settings, Log Changesswitch it off, or exempt with the reason
buffering initial, class C/G/E/Stechnical settings, Bufferingswitch on and choose a type
"allowed but switched off", small table (priority 2)technical settings, Bufferingswitch on, or exempt with the reason
buffering on, no typetechnical settings, Bufferingchoose single, generic or full
FLOAT in the primary key (priority 1)table fieldsuse a packed or integer type in the key

Conclusion

I used to treat this block of ATC findings as noise. Reading the class changed that: it's a short list of rules, each with a clear reason, and two of them are real errors that often hide among the notes.

Next time this block shows up in your ATC results, sort it by priority before you exempt anything.

Which of these rules have you seen the most in your projects?

entry.title: From clean core level to decision: reading what a custom program actually does (part 3)
entry.content:
Disclosure: I'm the author of this post and the creator of Clean-Core.io, a free, non-commercial community tool. This post is educational and describes a method you can apply by hand; the tool is optional and complementary to SAP ADT/ATC and the SAP toolchain, not a replacement.

In part 1 we graded each dependency of a custom object on SAP's clean core levels A–D. In part 2 we turned that into visibility and two KPIs. Both answer how far a piece of code is from a clean core.

Neither answers the question that decides the effort: what does this program do for the business, and should it be kept, rebuilt or retired? This part is about reading that from the code.

The business rules are in the IF statements

A grown Z-program is often the only up-to-date description of a process. Two passages from a fictitious purchase requisition approval report:

"Plant 1000 is the central warehouse
IF gs_eban-werks = '1000'.        " line 87
  gv_skip_limit = abap_true.
ENDIF.

"Tolerance agreed with purchasing
IF lv_dev_pct > 5.               " line 412
  PERFORM hold_for_buyer.
  RETURN.
ENDIF.

Neither is a clean core violation. Both are business rules: plant 1000 skips the approval limit, and a price more than 5 % above the reference goes to a buyer. Whatever happens to the program, these two rules have to survive, or someone has to decide on purpose that they don't. No ATC check tells you that. The code does.

A reading flow

Step Look for Write down

1. Entry pointsSTART-OF-SELECTION, selection-screen events, dialog modules, public methods, function modulesthe line
2. Dataevery SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, MODIFY, DELETE on own or SAP tablesthe line, read or write
3. Business rulesIF / CASE on business values: plant, document type, amount, tolerancethe line, the condition in plain words
4. EffectsRFC, update tasks, BAPIs, mails, files, messagesthe line
5. Gapsdynamic calls with a variable target, includes you don't have"not determined", with the reason

Draw the result as a process. BPMN works well because a key user can read it. Anchor every task and gateway to its line: a step that can't point back to a line is an opinion, and a gap you write down is an open question rather than a wrong answer.

Then add what parts 1 and 2 gave you: each SAP object with its level and how it is used. Reading EBAN is a different matter from updating it; a direct write to an SAP table stays a problem whatever the table's own level. And run ATC in your system: it is the check that counts.

From the reading to a decision

Option When it fits

RetireNobody needs the process any more. Usage data helps here.
Move to SAP standardThe standard covers the process; each custom rule maps to configuration or is dropped on purpose.
RebuildThe rules are still needed. Rebuild in-app on ABAP Cloud where the logic belongs to the core, side-by-side on SAP BTP where it is loosely coupled or mainly talks to other systems.
Keep for nowWith the risk and a review date written down.

One thing that is easy to get wrong: a classic construct is not by itself a reason to move a program off the stack. A batch input, a piece of native SQL or a local RFC call is something to replace with a released API inside a rebuilt in-app solution. Side-by-side pays off when the logic itself is independent of the core, not because one statement is old.

Record which option you chose, on which evidence (the lines, the levels, ATC), under which assumptions, and who confirmed it. Six months later, that record is what makes the decision reviewable.

What the reading gives the next step

  • Target design: which SAP objects the new code reads through released APIs or CDS views. Part 1 used KNA1 → I_Customer; for EBAN, look up the released purchase requisition API for your release on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.
  • A first code draft that carries both rules over, for a developer to review in ADT and check with ATC and the Clean ABAP style guide.
  • Test cases from the same rules, so "plant 1000 skips the limit" is a test, not tribal knowledge.
  • The process as a BPMN 2.0 file for whoever documents the to-be process, for example in SAP Signavio.

Where this stops

  • The code shows the process the code implements. Customizing, jobs and manual steps around it are not in it.
  • Static reading can't resolve every dynamic call. Say so instead of guessing.
  • The levels come from SAP's published data; ATC in your target system has the final word.
  • Generated code, from any tool or model, is a draft for a developer to review.

Conclusion

Levels and scores tell you how far a program is from a clean core. The decision about the program needs one more thing: what it does, line by line, with its business rules made visible. Read that first, and "we have a lot of Z-code" turns into a list of decisions you can defend.

How do you get from a clean core level to a decision per program today: key-user workshops, a decision log, something else? And where has reading the code misled you?

entry.title: Building on the ADT REST API: 8 silent traps I measured (and how to defend against each)
entry.content:
Over the last months I have been building tooling, and AI agents, that work with ABAP systems through the ADT REST API, the same HTTP API that Eclipse uses. And I noticed a pattern: most of my bugs were not in my code. They were places where the API answers 200, or "finished", or an empty list, and something else happened.

More and more people are building on this API now (agents, CI pipelines, custom tools), so I'm sharing the eight traps that cost me the most, each one measured again for this post in an S/4HANA 2023 system (SAP_BASIS 7.58). For each one: what you see, why it happens, the proof, and the defense.

1. "Finished" is not "clean"

What you see: you start an ATC run, the API answers HTTP 200 and the run is finished. Looks like a green light.

Why: the run status tells you the run ended, nothing about the code. The result lives in the worklist, and you have to go and read it.

Proof: I ran ATC on a test table whose log setting is wrong on purpose. The run finished normally. Then the worklist (GET /sap/bc/adt/atc/worklists/{id}) had this inside the object:

<atcfinding:finding ... atcfinding:priority="1" atcfinding:messageId="0022" .../>

(message 0022: change log active although the data class is APPL0 or APPL1), and an empty <atcworklist:infos/>.

Defense: after every run, fetch the worklist and count findings by priority. And read infos too: that's where checks that could not run show up. A check that didn't run is "not checked", never "clean".

2. A syntax check that didn't happen

What you see: you send source to the check run API and get zero messages back.

Why: if the object doesn't exist yet, the check isn't processed at all. Zero messages, because nothing was checked.

Proof: a check run with an artifact for a class that doesn't exist came back with chkrun:status="notProcessed" and the text "Ressource CLASS ... existiert nicht", and no messages.

Defense: read chkrun:status before reading the messages. Zero messages with notProcessed means "unknown", and a tool that reports it as "no syntax errors" is lying with a straight face.

3. Checking loose source uses default program attributes

What you see: a perfectly normal SELECT fails the syntax check of a draft program, and then works in the real one.

Why: "fixed point arithmetic" is a program attribute. When you check source for a program that doesn't exist yet, the check runs without it, while a program created in SE38 or ADT gets it switched on by default, and classes always have it.

Proof: the same SELECT, with a JOIN and an inline @DATA( ):

  • checked as a new program: "This ABAP SQL statement uses additions that can only be used when the fixed point arithmetic flag is activated", plus a follow-up error for the inline table;
  • checked inside an existing class: zero errors.

Defense: check code in the context of a real object (an existing class, or a shell in $TMP). When an error depends on a program attribute, treat it as a context problem, not as broken code.

4. Data preview: 255 characters per line, and 36 runs per session

This one is two traps with the same root, and the root is in the ADT code itself.

What you see: a long SQL in the data preview (/sap/bc/adt/datapreview/freestyle) is refused with "Maximum number of character exceeds 255 in line 1". And in a long stateful session, after many previews, you suddenly get an HTTP 500 saying that the maximum number of temporary subroutine pools was exceeded.

Why: the data preview compiles your query. Class CL_ADT_DP_OPEN_SQL_HANDLER, method generate_subroutine, splits the query at line breaks, refuses any line longer than 255 characters, writes a small program around it (class main, method EXECUTE_CODE) and runs GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL. The ABAP documentation of that statement explains the rest: a source line can't exceed 255 characters, an internal session can create at most 36 temporary subroutine pools, and they are never released until the session ends.

Proof: the 255 check is in the method above, with its own text element; the GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL is a few lines below; and I got the HTTP 500 after a series of previews in the same stateful session.

Defense:

  • send SQL with line breaks, never one long line;
  • don't run data previews in a stateful session that lives forever: use stateless requests, or start a new session before you get near 36.

5. An empty where-used list proves nothing

What you see: the where-used of a class comes back empty, or almost empty, and you conclude nobody uses it.

Why: the where-used list reads an index. For your own objects it's updated when you activate them, but the index for SAP objects is built by a separate job, which isn't always run after an installation.

Proof: in my system /UI2/CL_JSON calls cl_abap_typedescr=>describe_by_... in 16 lines. The global where-used index (WBCROSSGT) has zero entries for that pair. It has 611,981 rows in total, and only 69 for CL_ABAP_TYPEDESCR, a class the standard uses everywhere.

Defense: before you say "unused", run a positive control: take one usage that you know exists and check that the index finds it. If it doesn't, fall back to a source search.

6. Parse the element, not the value

What you see: your tool reads that every table type in the system is "sorted" (or "standard", or "unique"), no matter what.

Why: many ADT object bodies carry the editor's dropdowns. A table type body has the real value in <ttyp:accessType>standard</ttyp:accessType>, and next to it a <ttyp:valueHelps> block with every possible value: standard, sorted, hashed, unique, nonUnique...

Proof: in the body I read for this post, that block is more than half of the 5 KB. Bonus: its labels came in German, while my session was in Portuguese.

Defense: use a real XML parser and read the element that carries the value. A regex looking for the value anywhere in the body will match the dropdown and return a plausible, wrong answer for every object. And don't rely on the language of the labels.

7. A filter that is silently ignored

What you see: you call a list (named item) collection with filter=... and get a short list back, so the filter worked. Or did it?

Why: in these collections maxItemCount is applied on the server, but filter can be ignored without any error.

Proof: /sap/bc/adt/repository/informationsystem/objecttypes?maxItemCount=3, and the same call with &filter=ZZZNAOEXISTEMESMO (Portuguese for "really doesn't exist"), returned identical bodies, the same three items byte for byte. I had seen the same before on 7.56 and 8.16 systems.

Defense: test every filter parameter with a value that can't match anything. If you still get items, filter on the client side.

8. 406 means "wrong Accept", not "not there"

What you see: HTTP 406 on an endpoint, and you conclude the feature doesn't exist in that system.

Why: ADT negotiates the content type strictly. A 406 says the endpoint exists and doesn't serve the media type you asked for.

Proof: /sap/bc/adt/feeds with Accept: application/xml → 406, and the message lists the accepted type: application/atom+xml;type=feed. With that header: 200.

Defense: read the media types from /sap/bc/adt/discovery and from the 406 message itself before concluding anything is missing.

One more, if you are building agents

Everything that comes back from the system is data: source code, long texts, message texts, table contents. Any user can type a sentence into a document text. An agent that reads it must treat it as content to analyse, never as an instruction to follow.

The common thread

All eight have the same shape: the API answers successfully, and the meaning of the answer is somewhere else. My rule now is simple: for every "OK" a tool reports, it must be able to say what it read that proves it. "Finished", "200", "zero messages" and "empty list" are not proof of anything on their own.

If you have hit others, I'd love to hear them in the comments.

entry.title: My ABAP Escaped the Server, Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.
entry.content:
Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.

TL;DR: ABAP report on ZX Spectrum, CP/M, MOS AgonLight (ez80), and a mac.

I like JavaScript, and TypeScript too. JavaScript has become something of a lingua franca of modern computing, rather like BASIC was in the eighties: back then you could walk up to almost any home computer and find a BASIC interpreter waiting for you, and although the machines were different, the dialects were different, and sometimes even the meaning of PRINT was a matter of local tradition, you could usually get something running. Today it's JavaScript — in browsers, servers, desktop applications, little embedded environments, and places where you might reasonably wonder who invited it.

I love being able to take an idea and run it almost anywhere, and TypeScript makes the whole arrangement much more comfortable once the idea grows beyond a few hundred lines. But I also love Go. There is something deeply satisfying about compiling a program into a native executable, copying that one file to another machine and watching it run, without a dependency installation ceremony, a carefully reconstructed development environment, or a server that must be started beforehand.

After spending the last couple of months getting ABAP to run outside SAP with Open SteamGate, I began to wonder whether we could go a little further. OSG could already run ABAP locally, serve OData, work with CDS and connect to Eclipse, and I wrote an entire article about how a simple experiment had grown into something resembling an application server.

But what if I didn't need an application server at all, and just wanted to run a report? A perfectly ordinary ABAP report, with PARAMETERS, SELECT-OPTIONS, a selection screen, some Open SQL, a little file processing and WRITE statements at the end. Could I compile it into an executable and run it in my terminal — not start a server, not install a runtime, not connect to a development system, just run the program, and preferably have it stop when it finishes?

Well, yes, as it turns out. And then the terminal started acquiring features. 😃

The report that acquired a terminal

Let me show you where this ended up.

This is an ABAP report compiled into a native executable by osabap, part of Open SteamGate's new ABAP-to-Go compiler. The report still has its PARAMETERS and SELECT-OPTIONS, its INITIALIZATION and START-OF-SELECTION events are still there, and WRITE still produces the output; but instead of opening a selection screen in SAP GUI, the program renders it as a form in the terminal, where you can move between fields, edit values, toggle checkboxes and execute the report. The source is ABAP, and the result is a native executable.

I rather like command-line tools, so the next thing I wanted was to run the same report without the interactive screen. Parameters become command-line options, a checkbox becomes a flag, and SELECT-OPTIONS can be given as repeated values or as ranges. WRITE output goes to stdout, messages go to stderr, and the process returns an exit status that another program can understand, so the report can sit in a shell pipeline, a scheduled job or a CI run.

A classic ABAP report had become a CLI tool. The funny thing is that the report itself doesn't need to know about any of this: we haven't rewritten its business logic in a special command-line language. The compiler takes the report and its supported dependencies, produces Go, and builds an executable that carries the runtime it needs, so neither Go nor Node is required on the machine that runs it — both belong to the build. This is a growing implementation of a supported ABAP subset, not a promise that every report from every SAP system will compile unchanged; but for the reports that do compile, it is a rather different way of deploying ABAP, and quite a pleasant way of running it.

Naturally, I pressed F4

Once the terminal selection screen worked, I started doing what an ABAP developer does with a selection screen, and almost immediately I pressed F4. Of course I did.

If a report asks for a filename, you don't really want to type the whole path into a terminal field, and ABAP already has a perfectly good way of offering values for a field: AT SELECTION-SCREEN ON VALUE-REQUEST. So why not let it work in the terminal too?

And there it is. The terminal form calls the report's value-request event; when the report uses one of the supported frontend file dialogs, the terminal opens a file browser, you move with the arrow keys, filter with /, choose with Enter, and the chosen path goes back into the ABAP parameter as though this were a perfectly normal thing for it to do. The same machinery covers the file-open, file-save and directory-browse calls of CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES, within the supported terminal implementation.

There was one rather important question, though: now that the report could browse files on my computer, which files should it be allowed to see? The answer is only the directories explicitly granted to it, with reading and writing granted separately. The browser lists the permitted roots, and the DATASET implementation applies the same sandbox when the ABAP code actually opens a file, including paths it constructs without the browser. A file chooser that politely hides a forbidden directory is not much of a security boundary if OPEN DATASET can simply read it anyway, so F4 didn't just need a pretty interface; it needed to agree with the file-access rules underneath it.

 

The result is a native terminal application whose user interface is still described by an ABAP report. You can even serve the selection screen to a real SAP GUI over a local DIAG connection, although that is a separate, limited frontend mode, and the terminal F4 browser belongs to the terminal form, not to it.

So we started with a command-line executable, and it had now acquired a selection screen, value help, a SQLite database when the report has tables of its own, and access to files under explicit permissions. This was beginning to feel familiar. Fortunately, it could still exit when the report finished, which was becoming an important design feature.

The implementation and examples are described in osabap, and the F4 implementation has its own documentation.

But how did ABAP become Go?

The nice thing about working on top of Lars Hvam Petersen's abaplint ecosystem is that we didn't have to start by teaching a new parser the ABAP language: abaplint already understands an extraordinary amount of ABAP syntax and structure, and its transpiler already handles expression precedence and many of the language's complications. I wanted to reuse that knowledge rather than reproduce it, and at first the idea sounded like simply adding another backend: where the existing transpiler produces JavaScript, ours would produce Go.

This is easier to say than to do. JavaScript, Go and ABAP have rather different ideas about values, types and operations, and you cannot translate a method call into a Go method call and hope that everything around it behaves correctly. In ABAP the receiving type can decide how an expression is evaluated, so computing with the obvious Go types and converting the answer afterwards may already be the wrong calculation; moving values between structures has its own semantics; internal tables are not quite slices; references and method-local data have lifetimes that don't map neatly onto Go declarations; and, of course, there is SY, because there always is.

So the interesting part became the layer in between: a typed intermediate representation, or IR, in which the frontend has already decided what each operation means. The calculation type is known and conversions are explicit, so the backend doesn't look at an expression and improvise an interpretation of ABAP — it expresses a decision that has already been made. The path is roughly:

ABAP → abaplint parser → typed IR → Go → native executable

The frontend reuses abaplint’s parser and the transpiler’s precedence pass, then makes every ABAP decision once, in gogen’s typed IR. Two emitters spell that IR as Go or as JavaScript. From Go come two kinds of program: one report as a native command, or OSGo, open-steamgate’s own ABAP runtime compiled into one server binary.

Sources: tools/gogen/README.md “Shape” and “Language or model?”, docs/osabap-native.md, docs/osgo-release.md (“OSGo does not serve ADT yet”).

The generated Go uses a runtime library for the ABAP behaviours that don't belong to Go's language model, such as internal tables, conversion rules and session state. Once we had this representation, we could test it against the original ABAP behaviour, including recordings from a real SAP system, which mattered, because a compiler that produces a wrong answer very quickly has not improved the situation very much.

I would love to say that we got every rule right on the first attempt. We did not. Some of the differences were small enough to fit in the last bit of a floating-point value, and others were visible in whole frames of an animation: you might remember the mountains and the rotating tesseract from the previous article, and drawing the output turned out to be a remarkably effective way of noticing when two runtimes disagreed about arithmetic. Once the Go backend produced correct results for the tested subset, we started measuring.

Everything gets better with Go. Or does it?

The first numbers were encouraging. On a recursive Fibonacci workload the generated Go took about 0.24 ms, against roughly 24 ms through the existing transpiled JavaScript — about a hundred times faster — and a million-row internal-table workload showed a large difference too.

I am quite happy to accept arguments in favour of Go, but a hundredfold difference on such an ordinary workload is worth examining before declaring one language a hundred times better than another, because V8 is an enormously sophisticated piece of engineering. When we looked, much of the cost wasn't JavaScript at all; it was the execution model. In the existing transpiler output, ABAP values are runtime objects, arithmetic goes through the runtime's operations, and every method call is asynchronous, with async and await throughout the generated code. These are sensible choices for a general runtime that must emulate ABAP, but in a recursive workload each tiny call carries that machinery with it.

Our new IR had already worked out the types, conversions and operations, so we tried emitting JavaScript from the same IR, with plain values where the semantics allow it and synchronous calls. And here is the part I particularly enjoyed: the new JavaScript was dramatically faster too. Fibonacci went from about 24 ms in the transpiled JavaScript to 0.96 ms in JavaScript generated from the IR, and to 0.24 ms in Go, so Go was still ahead, but by about four times rather than a hundred; the million-row table went from 311 ms to 11.3 ms, against 8.7 ms in Go. Across the measured workloads, the new JavaScript path was roughly 7–28 times faster than the original transpiler output.

We set out to make ABAP faster with Go, and found how to make it much faster in JavaScript first. The same typed IR emitted as JavaScript, with plain values and synchronous calls, takes Fibonacci(25) from 24 ms to under 1 ms; Go adds the last step. One machine, two programs, not a ranking of languages.

Source: tools/gogen/README.md, “Language or model? The same IR emitted as JS” (measured 2026-09-23; 16-core x86-64 WSL2, Node 26.9, Go 1.26.0). The README has two more workloads (primes, a table of 10⁶ rows) with the same pattern.

These are measurements of particular programs and runtime versions, not a universal language ranking, and the gogen research notes contain the workloads, the environment and the numbers. What interested me was the explanation: the biggest improvement came from moving decisions into the compiler, instead of making the runtime work them out again and again.

Because the same IR can be emitted as both Go and JavaScript, we now also had two implementations to compare with each other and with SAP. Agreement between two backends is useful evidence, but the original ABAP behaviour remains the reference, since independent implementations can make independent mistakes.

There was one more twist: we compiled the Go to WebAssembly and ran it in a browser, and for the measured rendering workloads the IR-generated JavaScript was faster than Go/WASM, partly because the latter carries a larger runtime and different execution costs. So after setting out to make everything better with Go, we had made JavaScript better as well. I consider this an excellent outcome. 😃

And then the whole server wanted to leave

By this point, turning one ABAP report into a native program worked. But Open SteamGate already contained a substantial collection of ABAP classes, including its Gateway and the services behind the demo applications, so the next question was whether we could compile those too.

That is how OSGo happened. Instead of building one report with a small runtime closure, OSGo compiles the supported part of Open SteamGate's application-server runtime to Go: one native executable with the compiled ABAP services and their initial data, and SQLite through a Go driver. Start the binary, and it serves actual OData requests, with no JavaScript server process and no separate database server in that configuration. It doesn't yet provide every feature of the Node-based OSG host — in particular, it doesn't serve the ADT façade — but running the OData side as one executable was already a substantial milestone.

OSGo: the whole server as one Go binary.
 
A real OData request and its JSON answer.

There is something pleasing about compiling an application-server implementation written in ABAP into a Go executable and then using that executable to serve ABAP applications. It is a little recursive, but we seem to be getting used to that.

The report compiler gives us another practical possibility: ABAP programs that are useful without behaving like application servers at all. A report that transforms files, analyses data or runs a batch operation can become a native command with its own SQLite database, taking its arguments from a script or asking for them in the terminal, and the ABAP doesn't have to be rewritten just because its destination has changed. Once the compiler knows enough about a program, the place where it runs becomes a design choice rather than an assumption built into the language.

Of course, someone may reasonably ask whether this means my ABAP can run on a ZX Spectrum as well.

 
ZX Spectrum: FLEET.bin · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · sha256 2d52a6a2…dc74 · real capture, 10 s of emulated time, original 352×304 frames, no crop, scaling or compositing; not a benchmark. MZX emulator, Pentagon 128 model; the TR-DOS disk image is read through sector traps, no system or DOS ROM executed; no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP source as below. minz PR #203, merged.
 
 
CP/M: FLEET.COM · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · real capture, unmodified frames, about 8 s; Z80/MZE CP/M emulation, no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP report: F4 → FLEET.CSV → GUI_UPLOAD → typed table → cl_salv_table.
 
Agon: FLEET.BIN · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80-mode code on eZ80 · real capture, unmodified frames, real debugger pauses, not a benchmark. Both MinZ PRs are merged (#200, #201).

AgonLight2 (powered by eZ80) is quite a remarkable computer, by the way: AgonLight2 - Open Source Hardware Board

It can, a little. That is a different compiler, MinZ, with a rather smaller processor and its own adventures, including the occasional emulator that starts quite happily and then declines to execute the program we gave it. We'll get back to that one; I still have a terminal to show you.

Try letting your ABAP out

If you want to play with this, start with the examples under gogen in Open SteamGate. Building the native executables needs the development toolchain, including Go 1.26, but the resulting binaries can be copied and run on their target platform on their own. In a checkout, osd run compiles and runs a report in one step, and F8 on a report in VS Code does the same.

For an application-sized example, osg-demo has a chapter called My ABAP Escaped from the Server, which follows an airship-fleet report as its selection screen becomes a terminal form, its parameters become command-line options, and its local tables become a SQLite database. The fleet has been remarkably patient with this project, and I am beginning to suspect that the Old Boiler is less an airship and more an integration-test platform.

And I particularly recommend the file-selection example, zpickfile, because pressing F4 on a native command-line program generated from ABAP is something I still find entertaining.

And one more: F4 picks a CSV, cl_gui_frontend_services=>gui_upload reads it, and the report lists it with the headings from its first line.

BTW, does it look like R/2?

If you manage to break it, I'd genuinely like to know how. There are plenty of ABAP constructs and runtime behaviours still to implement, and a small report that behaves differently on SAP and on the native runtime is exactly what helps an independent implementation improve.

I started by wanting to run ABAP outside SAP, then without a server, and then I wanted the report's selection screen back. Along the way we ended up with a typed representation of ABAP, two code-generation backends, a faster JavaScript path and a Go application-server runtime — quite a journey for a report that only wanted to print a few lines. I still like JavaScript, I still like Go, and I now have ABAP programs that can travel between them, which is quite a nice place to be.

Except that, somewhere around the same time, I started working on another question. If we can compile ABAP into JavaScript and Go, what happens if we turn the whole arrangement around, take code written in TypeScript, and compile it into ABAP? And perhaps take an entire tool such as abaplint, written in TypeScript, and run it inside the very ABAP system whose code it was created to inspect?

It was not the first idea. Lars and I had been circling this question for a while, independently and not quite independently, each borrowing the other’s successes and failures in roughly equal measure. Lars went first with abap-wasm, a WebAssembly virtual machine written in ABAP: nearly everything compiles to WASM these days, so an interpreter for it on the stack opens a large door at once. I had spent some time on interpreters of my own by then — zork-abap runs Infocom’s Z-machine on SAP, cpm-abap is a Z80/i8080 emulator that runs CP/M programs, and there was a 6502 as well — so I thought a WASM compiler, rather than an interpreter, might be the more promising route. It turned out that WASM sits at too low a level of abstraction for the lift back to ABAP: you get a stack machine and a linear memory, and everything that would make the output readable has already been compiled away.

interpreting twice is interpreting too often - the fifth approach moves the work into a compiler

So I tried from the other end, with a JavaScript interpreter, which became ZMJS, a mini JavaScript engine in about two thousand lines of ABAP. It runs on a real system and even runs the abaplint lexer there. Lars then did the serious version, ZQJS, a port of Fabrice Bellard’s QuickJS engine to ABAP, which is a far more complete JavaScript. Both work. Both were too slow for the practical target, which was running abaplint itself on the stack, in a time a developer would wait for; an interpreter written in an interpreted language is interpreting twice, and that is at least once too often.

What I had left was the MinZ frontend. MinZ already lowers several languages — Nanz, MinZ, Lizp, Lanz, ABAP, PL/M, Pascal — into one high-level intermediate representation, HIR, before any of them goes anywhere near a Z80. So what if TypeScript and JavaScript were lowered into that same HIR, and then lifted back out as idiomatic ABAP? Classes, functions, closures and interfaces look remarkably alike across modern languages; the real differences are small and nameable, the main one being that JavaScript treats arrays as references while ABAP treats internal tables as values. Differences of that kind can be handled as explicit edge cases, and the rewrites that handle them are stated once in Grace, an S-expression language for rewriting and optimisation, rather than scattered through a code generator. That is ABAPiti, and it is where abaplint, written in TypeScript, comes back to the stack as ABAP.

Well. It seems ABAP was leaving the application server just as TypeScript was arriving.

They must have passed each other on the way. 😃

Next time: ABAPiti — A Journey Towards Self-Hosting.

Open SteamGate · gogen / osabap / OSGo · osg-demo · ABAPiti

P.S. I Ported SAP* to a 1976 CPU. It Wasn't That Slow. | LinkedIn - now it is true* =)))

entry.title: Changelog for SAP objects - Verify clean core level C compliance of your custom extensions
entry.content:
In the clean core level concept outlined in the Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud whitepaper, custom extensions using arbitrary SAP internal objects can be qualified as conditional clean core Level C extensions if dedicated pre‑upgrade checks based on changelog for SAP objects are executed for these extensions.

 Internal SAP objects can change at any point in time during an upgrade. Incompatible changes include, for example, deletion of objects, renaming or deletion of parameters or methods and others.

 To detect in custom code the usage of SAP internal objects, which have been incompatibly changed, SAP now provides the changelog for SAP objects, which contains the names of all SAP standard objects (and their associated components like methods or parameters), that have undergone incompatible changes in the new release. Technically, the changelog information is transferred via the Simplification Database infrastructure from the SAP Support Portal to your system. You can download it from the SAP Software Download Center of the SAP Support Portal and import it into your ABAP test cockpit (ATC) check system.

The changelog information is integrated and considered in the clean core ATC check Usage of APIs which can then detect in custom code the use of SAP objects and their associated components (sub-objects), that have been incompatibly changed.  

 SAP recommendation is to consider changelog during regular ATC quality checks to identify, early in the development process, any usages in custom code of SAP internal objects that have undergone incompatible changes. The changelog information should be included in the ATC check at the latest before the system upgrade, following the same approach as for the ATC checks related to the SAP S/4HANA simplification items.

 This will help to better estimate the risk of custom code not functioning properly after the next release upgrade.

Current functional scope

 The changelog provides information of incompatible changes affecting SAP APIs classified as released API, classic API, or internal API.

It focuses on the deletion of SAP development objects and their associated components (sub-objects) for the following object types:

  • Classes
  • Interfaces
  • Function modules
  • CDS views (DDLS)

 Deletions are reported as warnings for both the affected objects and their sub-objects. These include methods, attributes, types, method and function module parameters, and CDS view fields.

 The current changelog covers deletions introduced during upgrades from SAP S/4HANA 2023 to SAP S/4HANA 2025, helping developers identify potentially incompatible changes in SAP development objects and assess their impact on custom code.

Prerequisites

In your SAP S/4HANA 2023 or later system (private cloud or on-premise)  you are adopting the clean core level concept outlined in the Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud whitepaper and following the ABAP test cockpit (ATC) recommendations for governance of clean core ABAP development. You have already configured the Usage of APIs clean core check in your ATC system.

Setup

First download the changelog with the Simplification Database (SAP Note 3693326 (part 1)). As a result, the changelog.zip file is downloaded to your drive.

Next to enable the changelog functionality implement the relevant SAP Note 3758771 - Changelog Support in Usage of API ATC check.

Once the SAP Note has been implemented, upload the changelog content to the system in which the ATC check runs.

  • Remote ATC setup: Upload the changelog content to the central ATC check system.
  • Local ATC setup: Upload the changelog content to the local ATC system.

 PLEASE NOTE: If you are already using ATC on SAP BTP as your central ATC check system for your systems landscape, you can upload and use the changelog in your local SAP S/4HANA 2023 system, as the changelog functionality is not yet available in ATC on SAP BTP.

 To upload the changelog content on your ATC system go to the ABAP Editor (SE38) and execute the SYCM_API_CLASSIFICATION_MANAGR program (F8):

Click on the button Upload API File (Ctrl + F3), choose "Changelog" as a file type in the popup dialog and click on the Confirm. Select the previously downloaded changelog.zip file from your drive.

Once you see the uploaded file with data type "Changelog" in the Data Sources overview, the changelog is active and will report findings when running the ATC check "Usage of APIs".

NOTE: Only one file of the data type "Changelog" can exist in the Data Sources overview. To update the changelog, first delete the existing file, then upload a new version by following the steps described above.

How to use changelog in a pre-upgrade scenario

Execute an ATC run using any check variant containing the Usage Of APIs ATC check over your custom code in the system. In the list of ATC findings, you will see the issues related to the changelog, clearly recognizable from the Check Message text:

In the details of a changelog related ATC finding, you will see more information regarding your incompatibility issue reported by the changelog:

How to use changelog during development

It is recommended to consider changelog also during your development process. For this purpose your ATC check variant, used during development process, must contain the Usage of APIs check along with the changelog information.

In this example ABAP_CLOUD_DEVELOPMENT check variant is used in the development system, and the Usage of APIs check considers the changelog information. The changelog related ATC findings will be displayed with detailed check messages in the ATC result:

What’s next

Support for the changelog in ATC on SAP BTP is already on the short-term roadmap. The changelog approach for SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS and future SAP S/4HANA versions will be communicated soon.
